summary: Describes a simple mechanism for detecting data plane failures in MPLS Label Switched Paths. It has two parts: the information in an MPLS echo request and echo reply used for fault detection and isolation, and ways to send the reply reliably. It is standards-track and was replaced by RFC 8029.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4379 describes a way to test whether an MPLS path forwards packets as expected. A router can send a request through the path and use replies to check connectivity or locate a forwarding problem.

subtitle: A diagnostic method for checking and tracing MPLS label-switched paths.

tldr.problem: An MPLS path can stop delivering traffic even when the control plane does not detect the failure, making it difficult to find a black hole or misroute.
tldr.mechanism: An MPLS echo request follows the label-switched data path and carries information about the forwarding-equivalence class being tested. Routers validate the request and return an echo reply with a result code.
tldr.outcome: The method supports end-to-end checks and hop-by-hop fault isolation. RFC 4379 was obsoleted by RFC 8029.

today: RFC 4379 is a Proposed Standard and was obsoleted by RFC 8029. It was also updated by RFC 5462, RFC 6424, RFC 6425, RFC 6426, RFC 6829, RFC 7506, RFC 7537, and RFC 7743.

sections.title: Testing the Forwarding Path
sections.content:
An MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP) may fail to deliver traffic without the control plane detecting the problem. The RFC describes a diagnostic mechanism modeled on ping and traceroute to detect and isolate these failures.

The MPLS echo request is forwarded along the data path used for traffic in the tested Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC). In ping mode, the egress checks whether it is an egress for that FEC. In traceroute mode, transit routers examine the path and return information about forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: The test checks the path that packets actually follow, not only the route information held by control protocols. Replies can show whether the packet reached the expected egress or where forwarding differs.

sections.title: Echo Requests, Replies, and TLVs
sections.content:
An echo request is a UDP packet that may carry an MPLS label stack. Its fixed fields include a version, message type, reply mode, return code, sender handle, sequence number, and timestamps.

Additional information is carried in Type-Length-Value (TLV) fields. The Target FEC Stack TLV identifies the forwarding class under test. A Downstream Mapping TLV can describe the next-hop interface and labels so the sender can inspect downstream forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: The request names the forwarding class being tested and includes a sequence number to match replies to requests. Optional TLVs carry details that help a router check the path.

sections.title: Ping and Traceroute Operation
sections.content:
The sender sends a request with a label stack corresponding to the target FEC. In ping mode, the packet can travel to the end of the path. In traceroute mode, the MPLS TTL is increased across successive probes so transit routers can respond along the route.

A receiving router checks the request and reports a return code. The sender can use the response and downstream mapping information to form later probes and investigate alternate equal-cost paths.
sections.plainLanguage: A ping-style request tests whether the path reaches its egress. Traceroute-style requests cause routers along the path to report what they find, helping the operator narrow down a fault.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC discusses denial of service, forged or altered replies, and unauthorized use of diagnostic information. It recommends rate limiting requests and checking their source addresses against an access list.

Operators can also limit where replies may be sent. A reply can be checked against request information such as its handle and sequence number.
sections.plainLanguage: Diagnostic requests can consume router resources and reveal network details. The RFC recommends limiting who can send requests and how often routers process them.

sections.title: Protocol Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC assigns UDP port 3503 for MPLS echo requests and replies. It also defines registries for message types, reply modes, return codes, and TLVs.

These registries let implementations assign meanings to protocol values consistently. Vendor-specific values require the associated enterprise number TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: Registered numbers identify request types, reply choices, and results so implementations can interpret messages consistently.
